Why We’ll Have to Get Used to ‘Meh’ Job Reports
 
Plus, yen rallies and bonds stabilize
 

Good morning, I’m filling in for Spencer Jakab. Global bond markets are recovering a bit Thursday following a sharp rally in the yen. The currency is up around 1% against the dollar, and the yield on 30-year Japanese government bonds was down 0.10 percentage point to 4.07%.

Stuck in Neutral

 

The economy probably doesn’t need to generate all that many jobs to keep the labor market steady. But that won’t keep low job growth from feeling dissatisfying for many Americans, and challenging for investors.

 

Economists think Friday’s jobs report will show the U.S. added a seasonally adjusted 53,000 jobs in August. That would be a step up from July’s unexpected loss of 23,000 jobs, and better than the average gain over the previous 12 months of 26,000.

 

It’s still a lot less than people have been accustomed to—not just when the job market was bouncing back from the pandemic, but before it hit too. Over the five years ending in 2019, the U.S. added an average of 191,000 jobs a month.

 

What Friday’s report will actually show is a bit of a crapshoot. Temporary Protected Status ended for about 350,000 Haitians at the end of July, which could dent the employment figures. Any jobs people got hired onto for the World Cup are also off the table. On the other hand, July registered a large drop in state and local education employment that might have been due more to calendar quirks than anything else, and so could be unwound.

 

Stepping back from month-to-month noise, economists reckon the U.S. simply doesn’t have enough available young people to deliver much job growth. The population is aging, while the immigration clampdown has reduced the supply of workers. 

 

The plus side of that is that even limited hiring can keep the unemployment rate stable. Economists think Friday’s report will show an August unemployment rate of 4.1%, even with July and down a bit from 4.3% a year earlier. 

 

Relatively low unemployment aside, the labor-market environment probably doesn’t feel dynamic to many Americans. In the past, the low pace of job gains the U.S. is now experiencing has typically occurred just before, during, or right after recessions. Now it could just be a feature of the economy—some demographers believe growth in the working-age population will effectively stall out in the decade ahead. 

 

This creates a challenging environment for companies and investors, too. The U.S. business environment has always been underpinned by population increase—more workers, so more people earning wages, so more money to spend on cars and clothes and so forth. What will it mean if even in good times growth in the number of people with salaries to spend is at standstill?

 

The hope is that those salaries will be bigger—that artificial intelligence delivers on promised productivity gains, that a large portion of those flow into higher pay, and spending flourishes. But even if all that happens, it is hard to figure out what the contours of the economy will be, who will win, and who will lose.
